skills.search_text: kaplan-meier-survival-curve-estimation Use when patient samples have been partitioned into groups (e.g., network-based clusters) and merged with clinical metadata (survival time, censoring status), and you must test whether one group shows significantly worse survival (p < 0.05). Input is a single homogeneous cohort without group labels or stratification (no cluster assignments to compare) Clinical metadata lacks censoring status or survival time, so Kaplan–Meier estimation is not well-defined The goal is inferring the context-specific networks or clusters themselves rather than testing survival differences of existing groups http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Estimate per-group Kaplan–Meier overall survival curves and compare groups with the log-rank test, as applied in pyPARAGON's breast cancer use case to test whether network-based patient clusters from 105 CPTAC tumors differ in overall survival (Fig. 4C, Fig. S5). multi-omics/v1 10.1093/bib/bbae399
skills.summary: Estimate per-group Kaplan–Meier overall survival curves and compare groups with the log-rank test, as applied in pyPARAGON's breast cancer use case to test whether network-based patient clusters from 105 CPTAC tumors differ in overall survival (Fig. 4C, Fig. S5).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single homogeneous cohort without group labels or stratification (no cluster assignments to compare) Clinical metadata lacks censoring status or survival time, so Kaplan–Meier estimation is not well-defined The goal is inferring the context-specific networks or clusters themselves rather than testing survival differences of existing groups

skills.when_to_use_negative: The property is 1-D (per-cell or per-gene, e.g., library size, fraction of zeros per gene) — use MAD, KS, MAE, RMSE, OV, or BH instead of the KDE-based distance The goal is functionality, scalability, or usability scoring rather than accuracy evaluation of simulated data Simulated matrices contain missing or infinite values that have not been resolved, since the paper reports execution errors are mainly caused by missing/infinite values in calculations

skills.search_text: kegg-database-querying Use when an interaction table or node list uses identifiers from a source database (e.g. BRENDA EC numbers like 2.7.1.1) that must be converted to KEGG reaction IDs (rn:RXXXXX) or KEGG gene IDs before integrating with KEGG pathway maps. skills.search_text: kegg-pathway-overrepresentation-analysis Use when patient- or condition-specific inferred networks must be partitioned into functional modules and tested for KEGG pathway over-representation to reproduce cluster-level pathway frequency analyses (e.g., Fig. 4D Ras-module style extraction). skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw omics data matrix rather than an inferred context-specific network — network inference must run first (GGN construction, PPR flux scoring, subnetwork reconstruction). skills.description: Use when computing per-cell staining-intensity aggregates on large multi-channel images with polygon cell boundaries, where loading full raster masks would exhaust memory.
skills.name: lazy-image-bounding-box-extraction
skills.search_text: lazy-image-bounding-box-extraction Use when computing per-cell staining-intensity aggregates on large multi-channel images with polygon cell boundaries, where loading full raster masks would exhaust memory. Input is already an aggregated cell-by-channel feature table — no image or polygon geometry is present, so bounding-box extraction is unnecessary. The image is small enough that dense numpy raster-mask averaging fits comfortably in memory and a simpler dense-mask implementation suffices. No polygon representation of cell boundaries exists (e.g. only raw segmentation masks not yet vectorized) — Sopa converts masks to polygons before aggregation. Memory-efficient per-cell channel averaging in Sopa: instead of materializing full raster masks, cell-boundary polygons are spatially queried per image chunk and only each cell's small bounding-box region is loaded from the dask-backed (lazy) image, where the polygon is rasterized locally and channel intensities are averaged. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-48981-z
skills.summary: Memory-efficient per-cell channel averaging in Sopa: instead of materializing full raster masks, cell-boundary polygons are spatially queried per image chunk and only each cell's small bounding-box region is loaded from the dask-backed (lazy) image, where the polygon is rasterized locally and channel intensities are averaged.

The omics matrix Z is complete (no list-wise missing rows) — the complete-data LUCID workflow needs no integrated imputation The analysis goal is a standard one-exposure-one-disease regression rather than joint latent-cluster estimation across G, Z, and Y You plan to rely on impute-mice for high list-wise missing ratios (>0.5), where this paper shows drastic bias toward 0 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Impute list-wise (block-wise) missing omics data inside the LUCID integrated clustering framework rather than preprocessing with external imputation, using mclust-based regression initialization and EM estimation so exposure-effect estimates remain unbiased and clustering AUC stays stable as missing ratios rise from 0.1 to 0.8. multi-omics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae123
skills.summary: Impute list-wise (block-wise) missing omics data inside the LUCID integrated clustering framework rather than preprocessing with external imputation, using mclust-based regression initialization and EM estimation so exposure-effect estimates remain unbiased and clustering AUC stays stable as missing ratios rise from 0.1 to 0.8.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The omics matrix Z is complete (no list-wise missing rows) — the complete-data LUCID workflow needs no integrated imputation The analysis goal is a standard one-exposure-one-disease regression rather than joint latent-cluster estimation across G, Z, and Y You plan to rely on impute-mice for high list-wise missing ratios (>0.5), where this paper shows drastic bias toward 0

skills.description: Use when a multi-omics dataset shows list-wise missingness — entire omics (Z) rows missing for a subset of individuals — and LUCID integrated clustering of G, Z, and Y must still be fit.
skills.name: list-wise-missingness-handling
skills.search_text: list-wise-missingness-handling Use when a multi-omics dataset shows list-wise missingness — entire omics (Z) rows missing for a subset of individuals — and LUCID integrated clustering of G, Z, and Y must still be fit. Omics data are complete for all individuals — the standard unpartitioned LUCID EM applies and the likelihood partition adds no value. Missingness is sporadic (scattered cells missing completely at random) rather than list-wise blocks — the paper treats this as a distinct missing pattern requiring different likelihood handling. Only G and Y are available (no omics matrix Z) — there is no omics likelihood term to partition or impute. http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_3365 Extends the LUCID EM algorithm to list-wise missing omics by partitioning the likelihood: E-step responsibilities for missing rows (r_imj, Eq. 12) drop the omics (Z) conditional terms, and M-step updates of cluster-specific mu_j and Sigma_j use only the observed-omics subset {io}. The resulting integrated imputation yields consistent, less biased estimates than complete-case analysis. multi-omics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae123
skills.summary: Extends the LUCID EM algorithm to list-wise missing omics by partitioning the likelihood: E-step responsibilities for missing rows (r_imj, Eq. 12) drop the omics (Z) conditional terms, and M-step updates of cluster-specific mu_j and Sigma_j use only the observed-omics subset {io}. The resulting integrated imputation yields consistent, less biased estimates than complete-case analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Omics data are complete for all individuals — the standard unpartitioned LUCID EM applies and the likelihood partition adds no value. Missingness is sporadic (scattered cells missing completely at random) rather than list-wise blocks — the paper treats this as a distinct missing pattern requiring different likelihood handling. Only G and Y are available (no omics matrix Z) — there is no omics likelihood term to partition or impute.

skills.description: Use when recovering missing proteins in MS proteomics by combining multiple probabilistic evidence sources (prior, co-complex support, complex confidence) and you need a stable averaging rule that resists domination by extreme values.
skills.name: logit-space-equal-weight-evidence-averaging
skills.search_text: logit-space-equal-weight-evidence-averaging Use when recovering missing proteins in MS proteomics by combining multiple probabilistic evidence sources (prior, co-complex support, complex confidence) and you need a stable averaging rule that resists domination by extreme values. The analysis requires protein abundance, modification status, or subcellular localization — Protrec2 operates on a binary presence/absence basis and does not incorporate these The target condition involves novel or condition-specific complexes absent from the protein complex repository, or tissue priors that must reflect interpatient heterogeneity (annotations are population-level) The task is general differential-expression or enrichment testing rather than recovering unreported but biologically present proteins from a missing-value-laden proteomics matrix http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0128 Protrec2's Bayesian evidence-combination scheme: prior detection probability, co-complex structural support, and tissue-specific complex confidence are averaged with equal weights (alpha = beta = gamma = 1/3) in logit space, then mapped back to probability via the sigmoid, stabilizing inference so extreme values do not dominate. multi-omics/v1 10.1093/bib/bbaf692
skills.summary: Protrec2's Bayesian evidence-combination scheme: prior detection probability, co-complex structural support, and tissue-specific complex confidence are averaged with equal weights (alpha = beta = gamma = 1/3) in logit space, then mapped back to probability via the sigmoid, stabilizing inference so extreme values do not dominate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis requires protein abundance, modification status, or subcellular localization — Protrec2 operates on a binary presence/absence basis and does not incorporate these The target condition involves novel or condition-specific complexes absent from the protein complex repository, or tissue priors that must reflect interpatient heterogeneity (annotations are population-level) The task is general differential-expression or enrichment testing rather than recovering unreported but biologically present proteins from a missing-value-laden proteomics matrix

The goal is differential feature detection rather than ML sample classification — MultiPower's power calculation applies there, but its significance threshold and effect size parameters are not applicable to classification ER control No pilot data are available — MultiML cannot run without prior data, and parameters cannot be reasonably estimated otherwise Input omic data are raw or still contain batch effects — MultiPower/MultiML assume data have been properly preprocessed and batch effects removed beforehand http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Use the MultiML algorithm (R package bundled with MultiPower) to estimate the optimal number of samples a machine-learning classifier needs to reach a target classification error rate (ER) on one or combined omic platforms, as demonstrated on TCGA Glioblastoma subtype prediction with random forest at ER = 0.01. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-16937-8
skills.summary: Use the MultiML algorithm (R package bundled with MultiPower) to estimate the optimal number of samples a machine-learning classifier needs to reach a target classification error rate (ER) on one or combined omic platforms, as demonstrated on TCGA Glioblastoma subtype prediction with random forest at ER = 0.01.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is differential feature detection rather than ML sample classification — MultiPower's power calculation applies there, but its significance threshold and effect size parameters are not applicable to classification ER control No pilot data are available — MultiML cannot run without prior data, and parameters cannot be reasonably estimated otherwise Input omic data are raw or still contain batch effects — MultiPower/MultiML assume data have been properly preprocessed and batch effects removed beforehand

skills.name: macrophage-subset-spatial-interaction-analysis
skills.search_text: macrophage-subset-spatial-interaction-analysis Use when a task requires quantifying cell-type/cell-type and cell-type/niche spatial interaction via hop distances on a SpatialData object, e.g. verifying niche-specific macrophage co-localization in MERSCOPE liver data. Input is raw image/transcript data that has not yet been segmented and annotated — Sopa's spatial analysis operates on an already-annotated SpatialData object The analysis goal is segmentation or transcript/channel aggregation rather than post-annotation geometric/spatial statistics Data is not image-based spatial omics (e.g. bulk or single-cell dissociated data without spatial coordinates) Reproduce Sopa's cell-type and niche hop-distance spatial statistics on the MERSCOPE liver dataset to test whether macrophage subpopulations (LRP1, CEBP, TREM2) preferentially interact with themselves and co-localize in the necrotic niche, using a Delaunay cell-neighbor graph. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-48981-z

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw image/transcript data that has not yet been segmented and annotated — Sopa's spatial analysis operates on an already-annotated SpatialData object The analysis goal is segmentation or transcript/channel aggregation rather than post-annotation geometric/spatial statistics Data is not image-based spatial omics (e.g. bulk or single-cell dissociated data without spatial coordinates)

skills.description: Use when you have a single-cell MAPIT-score matrix (e.g., Supplementary Table 28, 1,499 cells × genes) plus co-profiled transcriptome and need to find cell subpopulations with distinct RBP-binding preferences or correlate binding strength with target RNA abundance across cell-cycle phases.
skills.name: mapit-score-matrix-clustering
skills.search_text: mapit-score-matrix-clustering Use when you have a single-cell MAPIT-score matrix (e.g., Supplementary Table 28, 1,499 cells × genes) plus co-profiled transcriptome and need to find cell subpopulations with distinct RBP-binding preferences or correlate binding strength with target RNA abundance across cell-cycle phases. Input is bulk MAPIT-seq data without single-cell resolution — the workflow depends on per-cell phase assignment and per-cell clustering; use bulk calltargets differential editing analysis instead The RBP of interest is expected to act uniformly across cell states — clustering on interaction scores is designed to reveal cell stage-specific RBP regulation, not global binding signatures You lack the co-profiled transcriptome; CellCycleScoring and score-expression Pearson correlations both require paired RNA abundance measurements from the same cells http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Cluster single cells on a cell×gene MAPIT interaction-score matrix (differential-interaction testing) and integrate co-profiled transcriptome phase scoring (Seurat CellCycleScoring) to identify cell-stage-specific RBP regulation, as demonstrated for G3BP1 in 1,499 scMAPIT-seq cells where a G2/M-enriched cluster contained 916/1,499 cells (61.1%). multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41592-025-02774-4
skills.summary: Cluster single cells on a cell×gene MAPIT interaction-score matrix (differential-interaction testing) and integrate co-profiled transcriptome phase scoring (Seurat CellCycleScoring) to identify cell-stage-specific RBP regulation, as demonstrated for G3BP1 in 1,499 scMAPIT-seq cells where a G2/M-enriched cluster contained 916/1,499 cells (61.1%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is bulk MAPIT-seq data without single-cell resolution — the workflow depends on per-cell phase assignment and per-cell clustering; use bulk calltargets differential editing analysis instead The RBP of interest is expected to act uniformly across cell states — clustering on interaction scores is designed to reveal cell stage-specific RBP regulation, not global binding signatures You lack the co-profiled transcriptome; CellCycleScoring and score-expression Pearson correlations both require paired RNA abundance measurements from the same cells

skills.description: Use when a MAPIT-seq run has produced a differential editing statistics table and you need to threshold it into a target list, or when reproducing MAPIT ∩ PAR-CLIP overlap counts (e.g., 4,769 G3BP1 targets in HEK293T cells).
skills.name: mapit-seq-edit-statistics-interpretation
skills.search_text: mapit-seq-edit-statistics-interpretation Use when a MAPIT-seq run has produced a differential editing statistics table and you need to threshold it into a target list, or when reproducing MAPIT ∩ PAR-CLIP overlap counts (e.g., 4,769 G3BP1 targets in HEK293T cells). Input is raw FASTQ or BAM alignments rather than an editing statistics table — use the upstream mapping/finetuning/callediting pipeline steps first The goal is detecting editing events themselves (edit site calling with REDItools2/SAILOR) rather than interpreting statistics to call RBP targets No orthogonal RBP reference set or supplementary expected counts exist and only site-level edit calling quality is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Interprets MAPIT-seq differential editing statistics (e.g., RBP_Edit_GE_RPE_DATA.tsv from the GATK-based callediting/calltargets steps) to call RBP binding targets using the paper's thresholds — editing fold enrichment > 2, MAPIT score > 0.5, adjusted P < 0.05 — plus Poisson (p ≤ 0.05) and coverage ≥ 10 editing-site filters, and to validate targets against orthogonal RBP reference sets such as PAR-CLIP. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41592-025-02774-4
skills.summary: Interprets MAPIT-seq differential editing statistics (e.g., RBP_Edit_GE_RPE_DATA.tsv from the GATK-based callediting/calltargets steps) to call RBP binding targets using the paper's thresholds — editing fold enrichment > 2, MAPIT score > 0.5, adjusted P < 0.05 — plus Poisson (p ≤ 0.05) and coverage ≥ 10 editing-site filters, and to validate targets against orthogonal RBP reference sets such as PAR-CLIP.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ or BAM alignments rather than an editing statistics table — use the upstream mapping/finetuning/callediting pipeline steps first The goal is detecting editing events themselves (edit site calling with REDItools2/SAILOR) rather than interpreting statistics to call RBP targets No orthogonal RBP reference set or supplementary expected counts exist and only site-level edit calling quality is needed

skills.description: Use when MAPIT-seq editing calls exist for both dual-editor and single-deaminase (hADAR2dd-only or rAPOBEC1-only) samples and you need to measure which enzyme configuration recovers more known RBP targets.
skills.name: mapit-seq-enzyme-configuration-comparison
skills.search_text: mapit-seq-enzyme-configuration-comparison Use when MAPIT-seq editing calls exist for both dual-editor and single-deaminase (hADAR2dd-only or rAPOBEC1-only) samples and you need to measure which enzyme configuration recovers more known RBP targets. No control (non-enzyme-expressing) sample is available, since calltargets requires treatName/controlName differential editing comparison The goal is identifying novel RBP targets rather than benchmarking sensitivity against published target sets Editing event tables come from a non-MAPIT-seq pipeline (e.g. plain REDItools2 output) incompatible with the calltargets binning/Poisson parameters http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 Quantify the sensitivity gain of the MAPIT-seq dual-editor fusion construct (rAPOBEC1–pAG–hADAR2dd) over single-deaminase configurations by comparing recovery of published RBP targets from 'Mapit calltargets' output, reproducing the paper's reported ~20–30% improvement. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41592-025-02774-4
skills.summary: Quantify the sensitivity gain of the MAPIT-seq dual-editor fusion construct (rAPOBEC1–pAG–hADAR2dd) over single-deaminase configurations by comparing recovery of published RBP targets from 'Mapit calltargets' output, reproducing the paper's reported ~20–30% improvement.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No control (non-enzyme-expressing) sample is available, since calltargets requires treatName/controlName differential editing comparison The goal is identifying novel RBP targets rather than benchmarking sensitivity against published target sets Editing event tables come from a non-MAPIT-seq pipeline (e.g. plain REDItools2 output) incompatible with the calltargets binning/Poisson parameters

skills.description: Use when paired-end FASTQ data from MAPIT-seq experiments needs alignment, abundant-RNA filtering, RNA editing event calling (A-to-G and C-to-U), or differential editing-based RBP target calling.
skills.name: mapit-seq-pipeline-execution
skills.search_text: mapit-seq-pipeline-execution Use when paired-end FASTQ data from MAPIT-seq experiments needs alignment, abundant-RNA filtering, RNA editing event calling (A-to-G and C-to-U), or differential editing-based RBP target calling. The goal is whole-transcriptome variant calling on matched DNA-RNA pairs rather than antibody-directed editing enrichment around RBP targets Data lack the hADAR2dd/rAPOBEC1 editing enzymes introduced by the MAPIT-seq protocol (e.g., standard RNA-seq without targeted deamination) Only alignment-free expression quantification is needed — the full editing-calling machinery (GATK, Poisson filters, coverage thresholds) is unnecessary overhead http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Execute the MAPIT-seq computational pipeline (WangLabPKU/MAPIT-seq, v1.7) to detect hADAR2dd A-to-G and rAPOBEC1 C-to-U RNA editing events from paired-end FASTQ data and call RBP-bound target transcripts, simultaneously profiling RBP-RNA interactions and the transcriptome. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41592-025-02774-4
skills.summary: Execute the MAPIT-seq computational pipeline (WangLabPKU/MAPIT-seq, v1.7) to detect hADAR2dd A-to-G and rAPOBEC1 C-to-U RNA editing events from paired-end FASTQ data and call RBP-bound target transcripts, simultaneously profiling RBP-RNA interactions and the transcriptome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is whole-transcriptome variant calling on matched DNA-RNA pairs rather than antibody-directed editing enrichment around RBP targets Data lack the hADAR2dd/rAPOBEC1 editing enzymes introduced by the MAPIT-seq protocol (e.g., standard RNA-seq without targeted deamination) Only alignment-free expression quantification is needed — the full editing-calling machinery (GATK, Poisson filters, coverage thresholds) is unnecessary overhead

skills.description: Use when you need a curated, functionally coherent seed gene set (e.g. genes sharing a MAPMAN 'Jasmonate' term) to validate a multiplex network with RWR_CV, and you must write it as a two-column set/gene file with matched negative/loosely-connected control genes.
skills.name: mapman-annotation-gene-set-curation
skills.search_text: mapman-annotation-gene-set-curation Use when you need a curated, functionally coherent seed gene set (e.g. genes sharing a MAPMAN 'Jasmonate' term) to validate a multiplex network with RWR_CV, and you must write it as a two-column set/gene file with matched negative/loosely-connected control genes. The genes of interest do not share a single expert-curated annotation term (MAPMAN/GO), so cross-validation would not test functional connectivity The target network is not a multiplex built by RWR_make_multiplex; RWR_CV requires an mpo multiplex object You need de novo gene discovery rather than validation of an already-defined gene set — use RWR_LOE seed-ranking instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Curate an expert-annotated gold-standard gene set from MAPMAN terms (e.g. 27 Arabidopsis 'Jasmonate' genes plus deliberately added non-jasmonate controls) in the two-column set/gene format required by RWRtoolkit, so that RWR_CV can test whether the set is topologically connected in a multiplex network. multi-omics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giaf028
skills.summary: Curate an expert-annotated gold-standard gene set from MAPMAN terms (e.g. 27 Arabidopsis 'Jasmonate' genes plus deliberately added non-jasmonate controls) in the two-column set/gene format required by RWRtoolkit, so that RWR_CV can test whether the set is topologically connected in a multiplex network.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The genes of interest do not share a single expert-curated annotation term (MAPMAN/GO), so cross-validation would not test functional connectivity The target network is not a multiplex built by RWR_make_multiplex; RWR_CV requires an mpo multiplex object You need de novo gene discovery rather than validation of an already-defined gene set — use RWR_LOE seed-ranking instead

skills.description: Use when fitting a SMOPCA-style Gaussian spatial latent-factor model to multi-omics matrices with spot coordinates, and the Matérn kernel lengthscale gamma must be learned by maximizing the closed-form marginal likelihood rather than set by hand.
skills.name: marginal-likelihood-hyperparameter-optimization
skills.search_text: marginal-likelihood-hyperparameter-optimization Use when fitting a SMOPCA-style Gaussian spatial latent-factor model to multi-omics matrices with spot coordinates, and the Matérn kernel lengthscale gamma must be learned by maximizing the closed-form marginal likelihood rather than set by hand. The data are very sparse and noisy or the spatial structure is very complicated — the authors warn that learning the appropriate lengthscale parameter may then be challenging, and manual user tuning may be required. You need to relax the shared spatial covariance assumption (Sigma_1=...=Sigma_d) across modalities — no closed-form marginal-likelihood solution exists, and the required orthogonal-constrained (Stiefel manifold) optimization was deferred to future work. The analysis requires raw-count modeling of dropout events and the mean–variance relationship — SMOPCA uses normalized data rather than raw expression measurements, so count-aware generative methods are preferable. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 In SMOPCA, all model parameters — the Matérn nu=3/2 kernel lengthscale gamma of the shared spatial covariance, and the modality-specific noise variances sigma_k and loadings W_k — are estimated by maximum marginal likelihood. Because the latent-factor model is fully Gaussian, the marginal likelihood is closed-form, so the spatial scale of the kernel is learned automatically from data instead of being hand-tuned. multi-omics/v1 10.1186/s13059-025-03576-9
skills.summary: In SMOPCA, all model parameters — the Matérn nu=3/2 kernel lengthscale gamma of the shared spatial covariance, and the modality-specific noise variances sigma_k and loadings W_k — are estimated by maximum marginal likelihood. Because the latent-factor model is fully Gaussian, the marginal likelihood is closed-form, so the spatial scale of the kernel is learned automatically from data instead of being hand-tuned.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are very sparse and noisy or the spatial structure is very complicated — the authors warn that learning the appropriate lengthscale parameter may then be challenging, and manual user tuning may be required. You need to relax the shared spatial covariance assumption (Sigma_1=...=Sigma_d) across modalities — no closed-form marginal-likelihood solution exists, and the required orthogonal-constrained (Stiefel manifold) optimization was deferred to future work. The analysis requires raw-count modeling of dropout events and the mean–variance relationship — SMOPCA uses normalized data rather than raw expression measurements, so count-aware generative methods are preferable.

skills.description: Use when clustering labels (K-means, Specter, Seurat, etc.) have been assigned to spots/cells and the biological identity of each cluster must be validated against known marker genes or proteins.
skills.name: marker-based-cluster-annotation-verification
skills.search_text: marker-based-cluster-annotation-verification Use when clustering labels (K-means, Specter, Seurat, etc.) have been assigned to spots/cells and the biological identity of each cluster must be validated against known marker genes or proteins. The cluster labels have not yet been computed or the low-dimensional embedding is still being tuned — verification is a downstream check, not a substitute for the clustering step No prior biological knowledge of expected marker expression exists for the tissue (e.g., novel tissue with no established marker panel) — then use unbiased DE markers instead Data are raw counts that have not been library-size normalized, log-transformed, and scaled — marker comparisons on unnormalized counts are unreliable http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Sanity-checks data-driven spatial-domain or cell-type cluster labels by confirming that known marker genes/proteins are upregulated in the expected clusters (e.g., CD3/CD4/CD49a in T-cell zones, CD21/CD23/IgM in germinal centers) before trusting benchmark outputs. multi-omics/v1 10.1186/s13059-025-03576-9
skills.summary: Sanity-checks data-driven spatial-domain or cell-type cluster labels by confirming that known marker genes/proteins are upregulated in the expected clusters (e.g., CD3/CD4/CD49a in T-cell zones, CD21/CD23/IgM in germinal centers) before trusting benchmark outputs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The cluster labels have not yet been computed or the low-dimensional embedding is still being tuned — verification is a downstream check, not a substitute for the clustering step No prior biological knowledge of expected marker expression exists for the tissue (e.g., novel tissue with no established marker panel) — then use unbiased DE markers instead Data are raw counts that have not been library-size normalized, log-transformed, and scaled — marker comparisons on unnormalized counts are unreliable

skills.description: Use when cells have been reannotated by Annotatability's reannotation module and you must confirm the new labels biologically by checking whether canonical marker expression (e.g., Gad1 for inhibitory neurons) now matches the reassigned cell type.
skills.name: marker-gene-alignment-validation
skills.search_text: marker-gene-alignment-validation Use when cells have been reannotated by Annotatability's reannotation module and you must confirm the new labels biologically by checking whether canonical marker expression (e.g., Gad1 for inhibitory neurons) now matches the reassigned cell type. Input is aggregated or convolved spatial transcriptomics data, which Annotatability does not directly handle No canonical marker gene is known for the cell type being reannotated, so alignment cannot be judged against expected expression The task is only to filter out erroneous annotations without relabeling; use the optional filtering step instead of the reannotation module Validates that reannotated cells from Annotatability's reannotation module have recovered marker-gene expression consistent with their new cell type labels, by comparing mean normalized marker expression (e.g., the inhibitory-neuron marker Gad1 in the MERFISH hypothalamus dataset) before and after reannotation. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s43588-024-00721-5
skills.summary: Validates that reannotated cells from Annotatability's reannotation module have recovered marker-gene expression consistent with their new cell type labels, by comparing mean normalized marker expression (e.g., the inhibitory-neuron marker Gad1 in the MERFISH hypothalamus dataset) before and after reannotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is aggregated or convolved spatial transcriptomics data, which Annotatability does not directly handle No canonical marker gene is known for the cell type being reannotated, so alignment cannot be judged against expected expression The task is only to filter out erroneous annotations without relabeling; use the optional filtering step instead of the reannotation module

skills.search_text: marker-gene-trainability-ranking Use when an AnnData object already carries per-cell confidence ('conf') and variability ('var') scores from DNN training dynamics and you need to rank genes by positive or negative association with annotation trainability, e.g. to verify erroneous annotations via marker gene expression. Per-cell confidence and variability scores have not yet been computed — run the DNN training-dynamics step (follow_training_dyn_neural_net plus probability_list_to_confidence_and_var) first Data are convolved or aggregated, such as that obtained from certain spatial transcriptomics technologies, which Annotatability does not directly handle http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Scores and ranks genes by their association with annotation trainability (confidence of DNN training dynamics) in single-cell data, identifying markers positively or negatively associated with correctly annotated cells using Annotatability's rank_genes_conf_min_counts. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s43588-024-00721-5
skills.summary: Scores and ranks genes by their association with annotation trainability (confidence of DNN training dynamics) in single-cell data, identifying markers positively or negatively associated with correctly annotated cells using Annotatability's rank_genes_conf_min_counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Per-cell confidence and variability scores have not yet been computed — run the DNN training-dynamics step (follow_training_dyn_neural_net plus probability_list_to_confidence_and_var) first Data are convolved or aggregated, such as that obtained from certain spatial transcriptomics technologies, which Annotatability does not directly handle

skills.description: Use when you need to test whether a spatially aware dimension reduction and clustering pipeline (e.g., SMOPCA on simulated spatial multi-omics data) is robust to kernel parameters, normalization methods, and gene-selection strategies.
skills.name: matern-kernel-sensitivity-analysis
skills.search_text: matern-kernel-sensitivity-analysis Use when you need to test whether a spatially aware dimension reduction and clustering pipeline (e.g., SMOPCA on simulated spatial multi-omics data) is robust to kernel parameters, normalization methods, and gene-selection strategies. Goal is benchmarking SMOPCA against competing methods (SpatialGlue, MEFISTO, TotalVI, etc.) rather than testing SMOPCA's internal robustness to its own settings Input data lack ground-truth spatial domain labels, so ARI scoring of the clustering against simulated domains is impossible Analysis targets non-spatial single-cell multi-omics without coordinates and you are not using the UMAP pseudo-spatial-coordinate extension described in the paper http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reproduces SMOPCA's robustness analysis (Additional file 1: Fig. S22-S31) by running the spatial multi-omics PCA pipeline across Matern kernels (nu = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5), three Seurat normalization methods (LogNormalize, SCTransform, VST), and SVG-vs-HVG gene selection, scoring each clustering with ARI against simulated ground-truth spatial domains. multi-omics/v1 10.1186/s13059-025-03576-9
skills.summary: Reproduces SMOPCA's robustness analysis (Additional file 1: Fig. S22-S31) by running the spatial multi-omics PCA pipeline across Matern kernels (nu = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5), three Seurat normalization methods (LogNormalize, SCTransform, VST), and SVG-vs-HVG gene selection, scoring each clustering with ARI against simulated ground-truth spatial domains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Goal is benchmarking SMOPCA against competing methods (SpatialGlue, MEFISTO, TotalVI, etc.) rather than testing SMOPCA's internal robustness to its own settings Input data lack ground-truth spatial domain labels, so ARI scoring of the clustering against simulated domains is impossible Analysis targets non-spatial single-cell multi-omics without coordinates and you are not using the UMAP pseudo-spatial-coordinate extension described in the paper

skills.description: Use when preprocessing raw TCGA-LUSC RNA-seq matrices for CanSeer: you have merged normal (N) and cancer (Cs) sample sets per use case and need 0-1 scaled expressions that feed patient-specific drug score (DS) computation.
skills.name: max-expression-0-1-normalization
skills.search_text: max-expression-0-1-normalization Use when preprocessing raw TCGA-LUSC RNA-seq matrices for CanSeer: you have merged normal (N) and cancer (Cs) sample sets per use case and need 0-1 scaled expressions that feed patient-specific drug score (DS) computation. Expressions are already normalized against a shared external reference (e.g. TPM/size-factor normalized for cross-dataset comparison) — per-dataset max scaling would destroy comparability between use cases You need to directly compare magnitudes across the cancer-only and paired/unpaired use cases, since the cancer-only case is normalized within cancer samples while paired/unpaired use the combined N + Cs maximum The input is a single-sample patient profile for downstream dynamical analysis rather than a cohort expression matrix to be scaled http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A gene-expression normalization scheme from CanSeer in which merged normal+cancer (N + Cs) RNA-seq matrices are rescaled to the 0-1 range by dividing every expression value by the maximal expression value; for paired and unpaired LUSC use cases the max is taken over the combined N + Cs dataset, while for the cancer-only case it is computed within the cancer samples themselves. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41598-025-99219-x
skills.summary: A gene-expression normalization scheme from CanSeer in which merged normal+cancer (N + Cs) RNA-seq matrices are rescaled to the 0-1 range by dividing every expression value by the maximal expression value; for paired and unpaired LUSC use cases the max is taken over the combined N + Cs dataset, while for the cancer-only case it is computed within the cancer samples themselves.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Expressions are already normalized against a shared external reference (e.g. TPM/size-factor normalized for cross-dataset comparison) — per-dataset max scaling would destroy comparability between use cases You need to directly compare magnitudes across the cancer-only and paired/unpaired use cases, since the cancer-only case is normalized within cancer samples while paired/unpaired use the combined N + Cs maximum The input is a single-sample patient profile for downstream dynamical analysis rather than a cohort expression matrix to be scaled

skills.description: Use when reproducing CanSeer's GDSC2 drug-sensitivity screening: you have per-cell-line, per-drug IC50 measurements, an LUSC cell-line annotation, and a list of candidate drugs, and need outlier-filtered mean IC50 per drug.
skills.name: mean-ic50-computation-per-drug
skills.search_text: mean-ic50-computation-per-drug Use when reproducing CanSeer's GDSC2 drug-sensitivity screening: you have per-cell-line, per-drug IC50 measurements, an LUSC cell-line annotation, and a list of candidate drugs, and need outlier-filtered mean IC50 per drug. You need patient-specific therapy-response quantification (drug scores, efficacy, cytotoxic effect) rather than cell-line-averaged drug sensitivity aggregates The dataset is not GDSC2 IC50 measurements restricted to LUSC cell lines (e.g. it is CCLE, PRISM, or a different tumour type), so the outlier-removal and reference-value checks do not apply Computes average IC50 values per candidate drug from the GDSC2 drug sensitivity dataset after filtering to Lung NSCLC squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) cell lines and removing outlier measurements, as performed during CanSeer's therapeutic screening. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41598-025-99219-x
skills.summary: Computes average IC50 values per candidate drug from the GDSC2 drug sensitivity dataset after filtering to Lung NSCLC squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) cell lines and removing outlier measurements, as performed during CanSeer's therapeutic screening.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need patient-specific therapy-response quantification (drug scores, efficacy, cytotoxic effect) rather than cell-line-averaged drug sensitivity aggregates The dataset is not GDSC2 IC50 measurements restricted to LUSC cell lines (e.g. it is CCLE, PRISM, or a different tumour type), so the outlier-removal and reference-value checks do not apply

skills.description: Use when several independent CRISPR/Cas9 screening cohorts must be aggregated into one consensus gene ranking to prioritize immune-evasion or ICB-response targets.
skills.name: mean-rank-gene-meta-analysis
skills.search_text: mean-rank-gene-meta-analysis Use when several independent CRISPR/Cas9 screening cohorts must be aggregated into one consensus gene ranking to prioritize immune-evasion or ICB-response targets. You have a single CRISPR cohort only — z-score/mean-rank aggregation across 17 datasets requires multiple cohorts to be meaningful Your goal is training the iMLGAM prediction model itself (base learners, ABESS feature selection, GA_train, risk scoring) rather than prioritizing immune-evasion target genes Your screens lack paired immune-competent vs immune-deficient conditions, so sgRNA read logFCs between those conditions cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Aggregates multiple CRISPR/Cas9 screening cohorts into a cross-cohort consensus gene ranking by computing normalized gene-level z-scores and mean gene ranks, then links ranked genes to prognosis via univariate Cox regression on a meta cohort. In the iMLGAM study this workflow ranked CEP55 first among prognostic genes associated with a high iMLGAM score (Figure 4B). multi-omics/v1 10.1002/imt2.70011
skills.summary: Aggregates multiple CRISPR/Cas9 screening cohorts into a cross-cohort consensus gene ranking by computing normalized gene-level z-scores and mean gene ranks, then links ranked genes to prognosis via univariate Cox regression on a meta cohort. In the iMLGAM study this workflow ranked CEP55 first among prognostic genes associated with a high iMLGAM score (Figure 4B).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have a single CRISPR cohort only — z-score/mean-rank aggregation across 17 datasets requires multiple cohorts to be meaningful Your goal is training the iMLGAM prediction model itself (base learners, ABESS feature selection, GA_train, risk scoring) rather than prioritizing immune-evasion target genes Your screens lack paired immune-competent vs immune-deficient conditions, so sgRNA read logFCs between those conditions cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when evaluating how clustering/prediction performance of methods for handling list-wise missing omics data degrades as missingness ratio increases, to select the most stable imputation-integrated clustering approach.
skills.name: median-auc-method-comparison
skills.search_text: median-auc-method-comparison Use when evaluating how clustering/prediction performance of methods for handling list-wise missing omics data degrades as missingness ratio increases, to select the most stable imputation-integrated clustering approach. Missingness is sporadic (element-wise) rather than list-wise, since the benchmark and integrated imputation scheme are designed for list-wise missing patterns in omics data The goal is only parameter-estimate bias/SD comparison rather than prediction/cluster-recovery performance, in which case a bias-and-SD-only design without AUC aggregation suffices The data contain no missingness, so no imputation-vs-complete-case comparison is meaningful http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking procedure that compares imputation/clustering methods (LUCID integrated imputation 'L', complete-case, impute-mclust, impute-mice, impute-EM) by the median AUC of cluster/outcome prediction across increasing list-wise missing ratios in omics data, as used in the LUCID incomplete-omics simulation study (Zhao et al., 2024). multi-omics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae123
skills.summary: A benchmarking procedure that compares imputation/clustering methods (LUCID integrated imputation 'L', complete-case, impute-mclust, impute-mice, impute-EM) by the median AUC of cluster/outcome prediction across increasing list-wise missing ratios in omics data, as used in the LUCID incomplete-omics simulation study (Zhao et al., 2024).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Missingness is sporadic (element-wise) rather than list-wise, since the benchmark and integrated imputation scheme are designed for list-wise missing patterns in omics data The goal is only parameter-estimate bias/SD comparison rather than prediction/cluster-recovery performance, in which case a bias-and-SD-only design without AUC aggregation suffices The data contain no missingness, so no imputation-vs-complete-case comparison is meaningful

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether segmentation of large image-based spatial omics data (e.g. Xenium, MERSCOPE) is memory/time-limited, or when validating that Sopa's patch-based strategy reduces peak RAM and runtime versus whole-image baselines.
skills.name: memory-runtime-benchmark-profiling
skills.search_text: memory-runtime-benchmark-profiling Use when evaluating whether segmentation of large image-based spatial omics data (e.g. Xenium, MERSCOPE) is memory/time-limited, or when validating that Sopa's patch-based strategy reduces peak RAM and runtime versus whole-image baselines. The dataset is small enough that Cellpose or Baysor already runs within available RAM without patching — the benchmark's memory savings will not be meaningful. The goal is segmentation quality assessment rather than scalability profiling — patching artefacts and ratio metrics do not measure segmentation accuracy. Input is not image-based spatial omics (e.g. already-segmented cell tables or non-spatial single-cell data); Sopa's patchify/resolve workflow does not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 Benchmark the peak RAM and wall-clock time of segmentation algorithms (Cellpose on images, Baysor on transcripts) run unpatched versus with Sopa's overlapping-patch strategy, quantifying the memory and time reduction ratios on large spatial omics data. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-48981-z
skills.summary: Benchmark the peak RAM and wall-clock time of segmentation algorithms (Cellpose on images, Baysor on transcripts) run unpatched versus with Sopa's overlapping-patch strategy, quantifying the memory and time reduction ratios on large spatial omics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small enough that Cellpose or Baysor already runs within available RAM without patching — the benchmark's memory savings will not be meaningful. The goal is segmentation quality assessment rather than scalability profiling — patching artefacts and ratio metrics do not measure segmentation accuracy. Input is not image-based spatial omics (e.g. already-segmented cell tables or non-spatial single-cell data); Sopa's patchify/resolve workflow does not apply.

skills.description: Use when analyzing annotated MERFISH spatial transcriptomics AnnData (e.g. mouse hypothalamic preoptic region with a 'label' obs column) to detect or fix erroneous cell-type annotations via DNN training dynamics.
skills.name: merfish-spatial-omics-analysis
skills.search_text: merfish-spatial-omics-analysis Use when analyzing annotated MERFISH spatial transcriptomics AnnData (e.g. mouse hypothalamic preoptic region with a 'label' obs column) to detect or fix erroneous cell-type annotations via DNN training dynamics. Data are convolved or aggregated spatial transcriptomics measurements rather than single-cell resolution — the article states Annotatability does not directly handle such data The goal is a standard Scanpy neighborhood/cluster analysis rather than annotation auditing — running sc.pp.neighbors overwrites adata.obsp['connectivities'] and replaces the trainability-aware graph Input annotations are probabilistic or continuous — Annotatability currently treats input annotations as nominal categories only http://edamontology.org/topic_3934 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Applies Annotatability's training-dynamics framework to spatial transcriptomics MERFISH data (mouse hypothalamic preoptic region) to benchmark mislabel detection against scReClassify baselines and to reannotate erroneously annotated cells so marker expression (e.g. Gad1) aligns with new labels. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s43588-024-00721-5
skills.summary: Applies Annotatability's training-dynamics framework to spatial transcriptomics MERFISH data (mouse hypothalamic preoptic region) to benchmark mislabel detection against scReClassify baselines and to reannotate erroneously annotated cells so marker expression (e.g. Gad1) aligns with new labels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are convolved or aggregated spatial transcriptomics measurements rather than single-cell resolution — the article states Annotatability does not directly handle such data The goal is a standard Scanpy neighborhood/cluster analysis rather than annotation auditing — running sc.pp.neighbors overwrites adata.obsp['connectivities'] and replaces the trainability-aware graph Input annotations are probabilistic or continuous — Annotatability currently treats input annotations as nominal categories only

skills.description: Use when a trans-omic interaction table (e.g. BRENDA allosteric metabolite-protein TSV) carries EC numbers in one column but the target pathway layer (KEGG rn map) requires reaction IDs, blocking cross-layer edge attachment.
skills.name: metabolite-protein-interaction-data-processing
skills.search_text: metabolite-protein-interaction-data-processing Use when a trans-omic interaction table (e.g. BRENDA allosteric metabolite-protein TSV) carries EC numbers in one column but the target pathway layer (KEGG rn map) requires reaction IDs, blocking cross-layer edge attachment. The interaction table already uses KEGG reaction IDs or KEGG-compatible IDs (transomics2cytoscape currently supports only the KEGG ID namespace, so no conversion is needed) The pathway layers are not KEGG-based (e.g. Reactome, Wikipathways, or SBGN layouts), since the package does not yet support those ID systems or file formats The input table's EC numbers are not in a single well-defined column (e.g. column 6) — column mapping must be verified before conversion or IDs will be silently misassigned http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Reconstructs transomics2cytoscape's ec2reaction conversion, which maps the EC numbers (e.g. 2.7.1.1) used by BRENDA-derived metabolite-protein interactions to KEGG reaction IDs (rn:R#####) so that allosteric edges and enzyme phosphorylation edges share one ID namespace with the KEGG global metabolic pathway map. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41540-024-00342-8
skills.summary: Reconstructs transomics2cytoscape's ec2reaction conversion, which maps the EC numbers (e.g. 2.7.1.1) used by BRENDA-derived metabolite-protein interactions to KEGG reaction IDs (rn:R#####) so that allosteric edges and enzyme phosphorylation edges share one ID namespace with the KEGG global metabolic pathway map.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The interaction table already uses KEGG reaction IDs or KEGG-compatible IDs (transomics2cytoscape currently supports only the KEGG ID namespace, so no conversion is needed) The pathway layers are not KEGG-based (e.g. Reactome, Wikipathways, or SBGN layouts), since the package does not yet support those ID systems or file formats The input table's EC numbers are not in a single well-defined column (e.g. column 6) — column mapping must be verified before conversion or IDs will be silently misassigned

skills.search_text: metabolite-trait-gwas-correction Use when running mGWAS of a pan-genome orthogene matrix against a large numeric phenotypic dataset (e.g. metabolomics traits per strain) and you must control false positives with trait-aware correction before nominating candidate genes. Traits are not numeric or not pre-processed per isolate (e.g. categorical phenotypes), since Scoary2's corrected workflow targets large numeric multi-omics trait tables The pan-genome has not yet been built — orthogenes must first be generated with OrthoFinder or Roary before association The dataset is small and per-trait correction is unnecessary — trait-wise Bonferroni at 0.999 is deliberately relaxed for high-throughput trait screening, not confirmatory single-trait testing http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Apply multiple-testing correction (FDR-BH and trait-wise Bonferroni) to a Scoary2 microbial GWAS that links a pan-genome gene presence/absence matrix to numeric metabolomics traits, recovering a controlled set of significant metabolite associations and top candidate genes (e.g. carnitine-related MFS transporter and α/β-hydrolase in the yogurt P. freudenreichii dataset). multi-omics/v1 10.1186/s13059-024-03233-7
skills.summary: Apply multiple-testing correction (FDR-BH and trait-wise Bonferroni) to a Scoary2 microbial GWAS that links a pan-genome gene presence/absence matrix to numeric metabolomics traits, recovering a controlled set of significant metabolite associations and top candidate genes (e.g. carnitine-related MFS transporter and α/β-hydrolase in the yogurt P. freudenreichii dataset).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Traits are not numeric or not pre-processed per isolate (e.g. categorical phenotypes), since Scoary2's corrected workflow targets large numeric multi-omics trait tables The pan-genome has not yet been built — orthogenes must first be generated with OrthoFinder or Roary before association The dataset is small and per-trait correction is unnecessary — trait-wise Bonferroni at 0.999 is deliberately relaxed for high-throughput trait screening, not confirmatory single-trait testing

skills.search_text: metabolomics-dimensionality-reduction Use when you have a metabolite-by-isolate abundance matrix (hundreds to thousands of features) and need to test whether samples cluster by a known categorical label, such as starter-culture taxonomy. The goal is association of the metabolomics traits with genes (use Scoary2 mGWAS instead), not unsupervised visualization of sample clustering. A supervised or classification model is required rather than exploratory 2D embedding of metabolome profiles.

skills.description: Use when a MultiPower run on a multi-omic design with Methyl-seq (or another high-feature-count omic) yields an inflated optimal sample size driven by low-effect methylation features, and you want to test whether filtering boosts power.
skills.name: methylation-effect-size-filtering
skills.search_text: methylation-effect-size-filtering Use when a MultiPower run on a multi-omic design with Methyl-seq (or another high-feature-count omic) yields an inflated optimal sample size driven by low-effect methylation features, and you want to test whether filtering boosts power. Methylation is not the limiting omic in the MultiPower estimate — filtering will not change the global sample size set by another platform Input data are raw or contain batch effects — MultiPower requires properly preprocessed, batch-effect-free data before any filtering is meaningful The goal is machine-learning classification sample-size estimation (use MultiML instead, where significance threshold and effect size are not applicable) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A dimension-reduction step for MultiPower sample-size studies: retain only methylation features with absolute log2 fold change > 0.05 before estimating the optimal sample size, so that high numbers of non-informative methylation features no longer dominate the multi-omic power calculation. multi-omics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-16937-8
skills.summary: A dimension-reduction step for MultiPower sample-size studies: retain only methylation features with absolute log2 fold change > 0.05 before estimating the optimal sample size, so that high numbers of non-informative methylation features no longer dominate the multi-omic power calculation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Methylation is not the limiting omic in the MultiPower estimate — filtering will not change the global sample size set by another platform Input data are raw or contain batch effects — MultiPower requires properly preprocessed, batch-effect-free data before any filtering is meaningful The goal is machine-learning classification sample-size estimation (use MultiML instead, where significance threshold and effect size are not applicable)

skills.search_text: microbial-phenotype-data-preprocessing Use when a phenotypic trait table contains continuous (numeric) columns that must be binarized before Scoary2 genome-wide association, and uncertain isolates (posterior probability < 0.85) should be excluded rather than forced into a binary label. Omics data are fully observed — the standard complete-data EM in LUCIDus applies and the likelihood partition adds unnecessary complexity. Missingness is sporadic (scattered entry-wise) rather than list-wise — the article treats sporadic patterns as a separate case the integrated imputation handles 'when necessary', so verify the pattern first with analyze_missing_pattern()/check_na(). The analysis goal is clustering on Z alone without G and Y — the partitioned likelihood's missing-subset component relies on G- and Y-related terms. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Derives and implements the likelihood-partition EM algorithm of the LUCID model for list-wise missing omics data, splitting the E-step responsibilities (Eq. 12) and the expected complete-data log-likelihood (Eq. 13) so that omics parameters are updated only from observed-omics rows. This yields an integrated imputation framework within LUCIDus that produces consistent, less biased estimates than complete-case analysis. multi-omics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae123

This yields an integrated imputation framework within LUCIDus that produces consistent, less biased estimates than complete-case analysis.
